name: Buenos Aires
info: Buenos Aires is the capital and largest city of Argentina, on the south-western shore of the Río de la Plata. A Spanish expedition founded it in 1536, and it became a viceregal capital, a port and a city of immigrants.

facts.founded: Established on 2 February 1536 by a Spanish expedition led by Pedro de Mendoza and abandoned in the early 1540s; a second and permanent settlement was founded on 11 June 1580 by Juan de Garay, who came down the Paraná River from Asunción.
facts.where: On the south-western shore of the Río de la Plata, in the pampa region of Argentina.
facts.known: The port of the Río de la Plata; the capital of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata; the May Revolution of 1810; waves of European immigration from 1880 to 1930; the Plaza de Mayo; tango; the dictatorship of 1976 to 1983 and the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo
facts.today: Buenos Aires is the capital of Argentina and an autonomous city, neither part of Buenos Aires Province nor its capital.

t: Mendoza's settlement of 1536 was abandoned after attacks by indigenous people, and Garay's refounding of 1580 became a port that depended on trade and, under Spanish restrictions, on contraband.

The city became the capital of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, began Argentina's independence with the May Revolution of 1810, and was federalised in 1880 as the seat of the national government.
From 1880 to 1930 it received millions of immigrants, mostly from Italy and Spain, and in the 1970s it suffered political violence and the military dictatorship that began in 1976.
dyk: The name came from the Virgin of Buen Ayre, the Madonna of Bonaria in Cagliari, Sardinia, whom Spanish sailors invoked for fair winds; for many years it was wrongly attributed to a Sancho del Campo, until Eduardo Madero's research in 1882.
ev: Pedro de Mendoza establishes the first settlement, in what is now the San Telmo district
Juan de Garay founds the permanent settlement
Charles III declares Buenos Aires an open port and makes it capital of the new Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata
The May Revolution removes the viceroy Cisneros and begins the Argentine War of Independence
The city is federalised and becomes the seat of government
The demonstration of 17 October at the Plaza de Mayo marks the emergence of Peronism
A coup led by General Jorge Videla begins the military dictatorship
The city elects its first head of government, after the constitutional amendment of 1994 gave it autonomy

sections.origins:
Buenos Aires lies on the south-western shore of the Río de la Plata, in the pampa region. The land was formerly crossed by streams and lagoons, among them the Maldonado, Vega, Medrano, Cildañez and White, some of which were later filled in and others enclosed in pipes. Parts of the city, among them the main port and the Puerto Madero district, stand on land reclaimed along the river's coast.

In 1516 Juan Díaz de Solís, sailing for Spain, was the first European to reach the Río de la Plata. He was killed in an attack by the Charrúa in what is now Uruguay. The city was first established on 2 February 1536 by a Spanish expedition led by Pedro de Mendoza, in what is today the San Telmo district, as the Ciudad de Nuestra Señora Santa María del Buen Ayre. The name honoured the Virgin of Buen Ayre, the Madonna of Bonaria of Cagliari in Sardinia, whom Spanish sailors invoked for fair winds; the chaplain of Mendoza's expedition, a devotee, suggested it. Indigenous people attacked the settlement, and it was abandoned in the early 1540s.

A second and permanent settlement was established on 11 June 1580 by Juan de Garay, who sailed down the Paraná River from Asunción. He called it the Ciudad de la Santísima Trinidad y Puerto de Santa María del Buen Aire, keeping Mendoza's name, and the short form Buenos Aires became common in the 17th century.
sections.growth:
From its earliest days Buenos Aires depended on trade. For most of the 17th century Spanish ships were menaced by pirates, and trade with the American colonies ran through convoys from Seville, the only port allowed to trade with them, to Lima and from there to the other cities of the viceroyalty. Goods took a long time to reach Buenos Aires, and the taxes on transport made them prohibitive. A contraband trade that the authorities tolerated grew up inside the viceroyalties and with the Portuguese, and it left a deep resentment among the porteños, as the people of the city are called, towards the Spanish authorities.

Charles III of Spain eased the restrictions in stages and finally declared Buenos Aires an open port in the late 18th century. He also split a region from the Viceroyalty of Perú to create the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, with Buenos Aires as its capital. In the second half of the 19th century customs duties, foreign trade, the fertile pampas and the railways increased the city's economic power, as raw materials flowed into its factories.

From 1880 to 1930 it was a leading destination for immigrants from Europe, particularly Italy and Spain, and the number of porteños tripled between 1887 and 1915, from 500,000 to 1.5 million. In those years the main avenues were built, the Colón Theater became one of the leading opera venues, and the first underground line opened in 1913. A second construction boom from 1945 to 1980 reshaped the centre.
sections.rulers:
Buenos Aires was under the Spanish crown from 1536. Spanish rule passed from the Habsburg period (1536 to 1700) to the Bourbon period (1700 to 1808) and the Bonaparte period of 1808 to 1810. In 1806 the British invaded and took the city, and an army from Montevideo led by Santiago de Liniers defeated them; the viceroy Rafael Sobremonte had escaped to Córdoba and named it capital. Liniers, chosen as the new viceroy, repelled a second British invasion in 1807.

In 1810 the criollo armies supported the May Revolution, which removed the viceroy Baltasar Hidalgo de Cisneros and began the Argentine War of Independence. The government was held first by two Juntas, then by two triumvirates and then by a Supreme Director, and independence was declared in 1816 at the Congress of Tucumán. Buenos Aires was never again under royalist rule. Its relations with the provinces were tense: the missions it sent out after 1810 to obtain their approval often ended in violent clashes. The city was the capital of Buenos Aires Province and for a time of the seceded State of Buenos Aires.

The question of its political status was fought out on the battlefield more than once. It was settled in 1880, when the city was federalised and became the seat of the national government, its mayor appointed by the president. The Casa Rosada became the president's seat. A constitutional amendment of 1994 granted the city autonomy, and on 30 June 1996 voters chose their first elected head of government.
sections.life:
Buenos Aires is laid out on a rectangular grid of square blocks 110 metres long, called manzanas. The city was conceived around the Plaza de Mayo, the colony's administrative centre: the Casa Rosada stands to the east, the Cathedral, on the same site since colonial times, to the north, and the Cabildo to the west. It is divided into 48 official barrios, a division originally based on Catholic parishes.

Most porteños have European origins, mostly from the Andalusian, Galician, Asturian and Basque regions of Spain and from several Italian regions. In the 2010 census 2.1 per cent of the people of the city, 61,876, declared themselves Indigenous or first-generation descendants of Indigenous people, and 15,764 identified as Afro-Argentine. The Jewish community of Greater Buenos Aires numbers around 250,000, the largest in the country. At the beginning of the 20th century Buenos Aires was the second-largest Catholic city in the world, after Paris.

Its Spanish, called Rioplatense, is influenced by the dialects of Andalusia and Murcia. The Italian immigrants, who spoke mostly Neapolitan, Sicilian and Genoese, created a mixture with Spanish called cocoliche, which declined around the 1950s. Lunfardo, a slang that began among the prison population, spread to all porteños and draws on Italian dialects, Brazilian Portuguese and African and Caribbean languages. Yiddish was commonly heard in the Balvanera garment district and in Villa Crespo until the 1960s. The Río de la Plata is known as the birthplace of tango.
sections.crises:
In poor areas health conditions in the 19th century were appalling, with high rates of tuberculosis. Physicians and politicians blamed the poor themselves and their crowded tenements, the conventillos. Floods damaged the city's infrastructure in 1908, and many streams were then channelled and later enclosed. The city was blockaded by naval forces twice, by the French from 1838 to 1840 and by an Anglo-French expedition from 1845 to 1848; neither blockade brought the government to the negotiating table.

On 16 June 1955 a splinter faction of the Navy bombed the Plaza de Mayo area and killed 364 civilians. It was the only time the city was attacked from the air. A military uprising deposed President Perón three months later. In the 1970s the city suffered from fighting between the left-wing movements Montoneros, ERP and F.A.R. and the right-wing paramilitary group Triple A.

The coup of March 1976, led by General Jorge Videla, escalated the conflict. The "Dirty War" resulted in 30,000 desaparecidos, people kidnapped and killed by the military during the junta's years. Their mothers, the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo, held silent marches. The mayor appointed by the dictatorship, Osvaldo Cacciatore, planned a network of freeways that called for the razing of residential areas; three of the eight planned were built. Democracy returned in 1983. On 17 March 1992 a bomb at the Israeli Embassy killed 29 people and injured 242, and on 18 July 1994 an explosion destroyed a building housing several Jewish organisations and killed 85.
sections.legacy:
The Plaza de Mayo, the scene of the May Revolution of 1810, has been a hub of political life since. Peronism emerged there in the demonstration of 17 October 1945, and industrial workers of the surrounding belt of Greater Buenos Aires have been its main support since. The city has also long been Argentina's main venue of liberal, free-trading and foreign ideas, in contrast to the more nationalistic and Catholic provinces to its north-west, and much of the country's internal tension, beginning with the centralist-federalist conflicts of the 19th century, can be traced to these views.

Its architecture is eclectic, with elements resembling Paris and Madrid and a mixture of Colonial, Art Deco, Art Nouveau, Neo-Gothic and French Bourbon styles. The simple Rioplatense baroque survives in the Cathedral and the Cabildo, and the Teatro Colón was designed by Francesco Tamburini and Vittorio Meano. The Palacio Barolo, built from 1919 to 1923, was the tallest building in South America at the time. On 30 September 2009 UNESCO declared tango part of the world's cultural heritage.

Buenos Aires is the capital and largest city of Argentina. Its population has hovered around 3 million since 1947 while the surrounding districts grew more than fivefold, to around 10 million. Cardinal Jorge Bergoglio, its archbishop, was elected pope as Francis in 2013.

summary: Buenos Aires, on the Río de la Plata, was founded by Spain in 1536 and refounded in 1580. It was a viceregal capital, began Argentine independence in 1810, received millions of immigrants and lived through the dictatorship of 1976 to 1983. It is the capital of Argentina.
references: Jason Wilson, Buenos Aires: A Cultural and Literary History (Signal Books, 2007)
notes: No 'History of Buenos Aires' file exists; only the city's own article was used.

PRE-1536 PEOPLES: the article names no people who lived on the river before 1536. It names only the Charrúa (who killed Solís in what is now Uruguay) and 'indigenous people' (unnamed) who attacked Mendoza's settlement. I wrote only that; I could not name the peoples of the site.
ABANDONMENT: the Etymology section says 1541, the History section says 1542. I left it as 'the early 1540s' and in facts likewise.
STATE OF BUENOS AIRES: the header list gives 1852-1861; the text says 1853 to 1860. I left the years out.
RULERS: the dynasty dates (Habsburg 1536-1700, Bourbon 1700-1808, Bonaparte 1808-1810) come from the article's header list.

30,000 desaparecidos is given as the article's own figure without attribution or range; I added no attribution because none is given. The editor may want a hedge from another source. The article says 'The dictatorship' without naming 1983 as its end except 'the return of democracy in 1983'; 'dictatorship of 1976 to 1983' in facts rests on that.

Left out: the 1994 bombing is given without naming the AMIA or who was responsible, as the article does not; the 2006 Cromañón fire; the present-day politics, economy, tourism, climate, sports, transport and twin cities; the 17th-century slave trade, which the article does not mention.
Population: 'hovered around 3 million since 1947' and the 2010 census figures are as given; the city proper 3.1 million in the lead is not used.
Palacio Barolo, Teatro Colón dates: the article gives the architects; the opening date of the Colón is not given.
